title: Imperfect subjunctive and hypotheticals
objectives: I can form the imperfect subjunctive of regular and irregular verbs from the third person plural of the preterite, and explain why the 'nós' forms ('-ássemos', '-êssemos', '-íssemos') carry a written accent.
I can talk about unreal or unlikely situations with 'se' + imperfect subjunctive + conditional, and say why that differs from an open possibility.
I can give advice with 'Se eu fosse você' and express past wishes and requests with 'queria que' and 'pediu que', explaining why the past form is needed.
I can express wishes with 'Quem me dera', 'Quem dera' and 'Tomara que', and use 'como se'.
I can give both the word-for-word meaning and the natural translation of the fixed phrases of this unit.

vocabulary.note: Written 'nh', which is one sound like 'ny' in 'canyon' (first lesson). Ends in 'o', so the stress is on the second to last syllable: SO-nho.

example.target: Meu sonho era morar no exterior.
example.source: My dream was to live abroad.

vocabulary.note: A reflexive verb, which means the action turns back on the subject: the 'se' is the same reflexive pronoun as in 'se levantar'. The verb literally says 'to repent oneself', which is why Portuguese needs 'se' where English 'regret' does not. The 'rr' is one strong 'r' sound, and the 'n' of 'en' is not a consonant here: it only nasalizes the 'e'.

example.target: Ela se arrependeu da decisão.
example.source: She regretted the decision.

vocabulary.note: The noun from 'arrepender', made with the ending '-mento', which turns a verb into a noun ('pensar' gives 'pensamento'). The 'rr' is the strong 'r'. The ending 'o' predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so ar-re-pen-di-MEN-to needs no accent.

example.target: O maior arrependimento dele foi não viajar mais.
example.source: His greatest regret was not traveling more.

vocabulary.note: Fixed exclamation of longing. 'Dera' is an old one-word form of 'dar' meaning 'had given', which survives mostly in fixed phrases like this one, so the phrase literally asks 'who had given me this', said about something nobody has given or will give. Followed by an infinitive when the wisher would also do or have the thing, or by a clause (a group of words with its own subject and verb) in the imperfect subjunctive. In 'quem', 'qu' before 'e' is a 'k' sound and the 'u' is silent.

example.target: Quem me dera ter mais tempo livre!
example.source: If only I had more free time!
example.source_literal: Who to-me had-given to-have more free time!

vocabulary.note: Short form of 'quem me dera', with the same meaning and the same literal sense of 'who had given'. Usually followed by a subject and the imperfect subjunctive, explained in the grammar notes.

example.target: Quem dera eu pudesse viajar todo mês.
example.source: If only I could travel every month.
example.source_literal: Who had-given I could travel every month.

vocabulary.note: Followed by the imperfect subjunctive, because it compares reality with an imagined situation that is simultaneous with the main verb (see the last grammar note).

example.target: Ela fala como se soubesse tudo.
example.source: She talks as if she knew everything.

vocabulary.note: The final 'i' and 'a' are separate syllables: lo-te-RI-a. The stress is on the 'i', the second to last syllable, which is what the ending 'a' predicts, so no accent is written. It works like 'tia'.

example.target: Se eu ganhasse na loteria, compraria uma casa.
example.source: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.

vocabulary.note: Stress on the last syllable, which is the default for a word ending in 'r', so no accent. The 't' before 'i' sounds like 'ch' in 'cheese', as in the first lesson.

example.target: Se eu tivesse dinheiro, investiria em um negócio.
example.source: If I had money, I would invest in a business.

vocabulary.note: Means to save money by spending less; it is not used for saving a file or saving someone's life. The 'z' is a 'z' sound, and the final 'r' gives the default stress on the last syllable: e-co-no-mi-ZAR.

example.target: Se eu economizasse mais, viajaria no fim do ano.
example.source: If I saved more, I would travel at the end of the year.

vocabulary.note: DÍ-vi-da is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so it carries the acute accent. The 'd' before 'i' sounds like 'j' in 'judge'.

example.target: Se eu não tivesse dívidas, me sentiria mais livre.
example.source: If I had no debts, I would feel freer.

vocabulary.note: The ending 'io' counts the 'i' as its own syllable: sa-LÁ-ri-o. The stress is on the third to last syllable, so the acute accent is required.

example.target: Se meu salário fosse maior, eu moraria sozinho.
example.source: If my salary were higher, I would live alone.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on 'da' (second to last, as the ending 'e' predicts), so no accent. The final 'de' sounds like 'jee'.

example.target: Se eu tivesse a oportunidade, viveria no exterior.
example.source: If I had the opportunity, I would live abroad.

vocabulary.note: 'Tomar uma decisão', literally 'to take a decision', is the usual way to say to make a decision. The ending 'ão' is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone is enough. The 's' between two vowels is a 'z' sound, and the 'c' before 'i' is an 's' sound.

example.target: Se eu fosse você, tomaria essa decisão com calma.
example.source: If I were you, I would make that decision calmly.
example.source_literal: If I were you, I-would-take this decision with calm.

vocabulary.source: to risk, to take a chance
vocabulary.note: The 'rr' is the strong 'r'. The 'c' before 'a' is a 'k' sound, so the 's' and 'c' together sound like 'sk'.

example.target: Se eu fosse mais corajoso, arriscaria mais.
example.source: If I were braver, I would take more chances.

vocabulary.note: 'Pena' means pain, sorrow or pity, so the idea is that the result is worth the trouble. 'Valer' is irregular in the 'eu' form of the present ('eu valho', but 'ele vale'), while the imperfect subjunctive follows the recipe from the preterite 'valeram': 'valesse'.

example.target: Se valesse a pena, eu faria o curso.
example.source: If it were worth it, I would take the course.

vocabulary.note: The standard way to introduce advice. 'Fosse' is the imperfect subjunctive of 'ser'; its stressed 'o' is open, like 'aw' in 'law'. The clause is unreal because the speaker is not the listener.

example.target: Se eu fosse você, aceitaria o emprego.
example.source: If I were you, I would accept the job.

vocabulary.note: Used in 'morar no exterior', 'viajar para o exterior'. The 'x' before a consonant sounds like 's', so the first syllable sounds like 'ess'.

example.target: Se eu morasse no exterior, sentiria saudade da comida.
example.source: If I lived abroad, I would miss the food.

vocabulary.source: to quit, to drop, to let go of
vocabulary.note: Colloquial and very common: 'largar o emprego', 'largar o cigarro'. The 'g' before 'a' is a hard 'g', which is why the conditional is written 'largaria', with no change of spelling.

example.target: Se eu fosse você, não largaria o emprego agora.
example.source: If I were you, I wouldn't quit the job now.

vocabulary.note: 'Abrir' is literally to open, used for starting a business much as English says to open a shop. 'Negócio' is stressed on the third to last syllable, ne-GÓ-ci-o, so it carries the acute accent, which also marks the open 'o'.

example.target: Se eu tivesse capital, abriria um negócio.
example.source: If I had capital, I would start a business.

example.target: Se eu tivesse mais tempo livre, aprenderia a tocar violão.
example.source: If I had more free time, I would learn to play the guitar.

vocabulary.note: In 'tempo', the 'em' before 'p' is a nasal vowel. In 'livre', the 'r' after 'v' is a tap and the final 'e' is said like 'ee'.
'Ficar' is literally to stay or remain; before an adjective it means to become. The 'c' before 'a' is a 'k' sound.

example.target: Se eu ficasse rico, ajudaria minha família.
example.source: If I got rich, I would help my family.
example.source_literal: If I stayed rich, I-would-help my family.

vocabulary.note: 'Seria' is the conditional of 'ser'. It is stressed on the 'i' (se-RI-a), which the ending 'a' predicts, so no accent is written. Portuguese leaves out the subject 'it', which English must supply.

example.target: Seria bom se a gente pudesse viajar mais.
example.source: It would be good if we could travel more.
example.source_literal: Would-be good if the-people could travel more.

dialogues.title: E se a gente ganhasse na loteria?
dialogues.context: Three friends have lunch together and play the game of what they would do with a lottery prize.

lines.speaker: Natália
lines.target: Gente, se vocês ganhassem na loteria, o que fariam?
lines.source: Guys, if you won the lottery, what would you do?
lines.source_literal: People, if you-all won in-the lottery, what would-you-all-do?

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Eu largaria o emprego no mesmo dia e viajaria pelo mundo.
lines.source: I would quit my job the same day and travel around the world.
lines.source_literal: I would-let-go-of the job on-the same day and would-travel through-the world.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.target: Eu não largaria. Se eu tivesse todo esse dinheiro, abriria um negócio.
lines.source: I wouldn't quit. If I had all that money, I would start a business.

lines.speaker: Natália
lines.target: Que tipo de negócio?
lines.source: What kind of business?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.target: Uma padaria. Quem me dera ter coragem de abrir uma agora!
lines.source: A bakery. If only I had the courage to open one now!
lines.source_literal: A bakery. Who to-me had-given to-have courage to open one now!

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Se eu fosse você, começaria pequeno, só com um carrinho de café.
lines.source: If I were you, I would start small, just with a coffee cart.
lines.source_literal: If I were you, I-would-start small, only with a little-cart of coffee.

lines.speaker: Natália
lines.target: Eu compraria uma casinha na praia e viveria com calma.
lines.source: I would buy a little house on the beach and live peacefully.
lines.source_literal: I would-buy a little-house on-the beach and would-live with calm.

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Quem dera a gente pudesse fazer isso de verdade.
lines.source: If only we could really do that.
lines.source_literal: Who had-given the-people could do this of truth.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.target: Se a gente economizasse um pouco mais, talvez desse certo.
lines.source: If we saved a little more, maybe it would work out.
lines.source_literal: If the-people saved a little more, maybe it-gave right.

lines.speaker: Natália
lines.target: Então vamos começar a guardar dinheiro hoje!
lines.source: Then let's start saving money today!
lines.source_literal: Then we-go to-begin to keep money today!

dialogues.title: Uma proposta em Lisboa
dialogues.context: Priscila has been offered a job in Lisbon and asks her friend Eduardo for advice.

lines.speaker: Priscila
lines.target: Eduardo, recebi uma proposta de emprego em Lisboa. Não sei o que fazer.
lines.source: Eduardo, I received a job offer in Lisbon. I don't know what to do.
lines.source_literal: Eduardo, I-received a proposal of job in Lisbon. Not I-know what to-do.

lines.speaker: Eduardo
lines.target: Se eu fosse você, aceitaria. É uma grande oportunidade.
lines.source: If I were you, I would accept. It's a great opportunity.

lines.speaker: Priscila
lines.target: Mas eu queria que minha família pudesse ir comigo.
lines.source: But I wish my family could go with me.
lines.source_literal: But I wanted that my family could go with-me.

lines.speaker: Eduardo
lines.target: Entendo. Se eles pudessem, iriam sem pensar. Mas vocês podem conversar pelo celular todo dia.
lines.source: I understand. If they could, they would go without thinking. But you can talk on the phone every day.
lines.source_literal: I-understand. If they could, they-would-go without thinking. But you-all can talk by-the cellphone all day.

lines.speaker: Priscila
lines.target: Meu pai pediu que eu pensasse bem antes de decidir.
lines.source: My father asked me to think carefully before deciding.
lines.source_literal: My father asked that I thought well before of deciding.

lines.speaker: Eduardo
lines.target: Ele tem razão. Se eu estivesse no seu lugar, faria uma lista de prós e contras.
lines.source: He's right. If I were in your place, I would make a list of pros and cons.
lines.source_literal: He has reason. If I were in-the your place, I-would-make a list of pros and cons.

lines.speaker: Priscila
lines.target: Boa ideia. E o salário? Se fosse menor, eu não aceitaria.
lines.source: Good idea. And the salary? If it were lower, I wouldn't accept.

lines.speaker: Eduardo
lines.target: Mas é maior! Se você ficasse aqui, demoraria anos para ganhar isso.
lines.source: But it's higher! If you stayed here, it would take years to earn that.
lines.source_literal: But it-is bigger! If you stayed here, it-would-delay years to earn this.

lines.speaker: Priscila
lines.target: Tá bom, vou decidir até sexta. Obrigada pelo conselho.
lines.source: Okay, I'll decide by Friday. Thanks for the advice.
lines.source_literal: Is good, I-go to-decide until Friday. Thankful for-the advice.

dialogues.title: Arrependimentos e sonhos
dialogues.context: Sérgio and Renata, both in their forties, talk about the lives they might have lived.

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.target: Sérgio, você já pensou em como seria sua vida se fosse músico?
lines.source: Sérgio, have you ever thought about what your life would be like if you were a musician?
lines.source_literal: Sérgio, you already thought in how would-be your life if you-were musician?

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Penso sempre. Se eu fosse músico, estaria tocando em algum bar agora, e não trabalhando num escritório.
lines.source: All the time. If I were a musician, I would be playing in some bar now, and not working in an office.
lines.source_literal: I-think always. If I were musician, I-would-be playing in some bar now, and not working in-an office.

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.target: Você ainda toca violão?
lines.source: Do you still play the guitar?

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Pouco. Se eu tivesse mais tempo livre, tocaria todo dia.
lines.source: Little. If I had more free time, I would play every day.

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.target: Eu também tenho meus arrependimentos. Eu queria que meus pais me deixassem morar no exterior quando eu era jovem.
lines.source: I have my regrets too. I wanted my parents to let me live abroad when I was young.
lines.source_literal: I also have my regrets. I wanted that my parents me let live in-the abroad when I was young.

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Ah, quem dera a gente pudesse voltar no tempo!
lines.source: Ah, if only we could go back in time!
lines.source_literal: Ah, who had-given the-people could return in-the time!

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.target: Seria bom, né? Mas as pessoas falam como se fosse simples mudar de vida depois dos quarenta.
lines.source: That would be nice, right? But people talk as if it were simple to change your life after forty.
lines.source_literal: Would-be good, no? But the people speak as if were simple to-change of life after of-the forty.

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Não é impossível. Se você quisesse, ainda poderia viajar por um ano.
lines.source: It's not impossible. If you wanted to, you could still travel for a year.

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.target: Quem sabe. Vou pensar nisso com calma.
lines.source: Who knows. I'll think about it calmly.
lines.source_literal: Who knows. I-go to-think in-this with calm.

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Pense mesmo. Ninguém deveria viver com arrependimento.
lines.source: Do think about it. Nobody should live with regret.
lines.source_literal: Think same. Nobody should live with regret.

grammar.title: What the imperfect subjunctive is, and how it is formed
grammar.explanation:
A mood is the attitude a verb form takes toward what it says: the indicative presents something as a fact, and the subjunctive presents it as wished for, doubted, imagined or not yet real. You already know two subjunctive tenses, the present subjunctive ('Quero que você venha') and the future subjunctive ('Quando eu chegar'). The imperfect subjunctive, in Portuguese 'imperfeito do subjuntivo', is the third, and it has two jobs. First, it describes an imagined situation that is untrue or unlikely: 'Se eu fosse rico' (If I were rich). Second, it is the subjunctive seen from a point in the past: 'Eu queria que você viesse' (I wanted you to come). The next notes teach each job; this note teaches the form.

English does both jobs with a borrowed past. In 'If I had money' and 'I wish he were here' the verbs 'had' and 'were' are past forms, although nothing is in the past: the past form signals distance from reality. English has almost lost the separate subjunctive: only 'were' ('If I were you', rather than 'If I was you') still differs from the plain past, and for every other verb, such as 'had' or 'spoke', the mood is invisible. Portuguese keeps a dedicated set of forms for every verb. The name imperfect subjunctive has nothing to do with the imperfect indicative ('falava', 'comia'), which describes habits and backgrounds. 'Falava' is 'she used to speak', a fact; 'falasse' is 'if she spoke', an imagined case.

The recipe is the one that built the future subjunctive. The preterite is the simple past for a completed event, and its 'eles' form ('falaram', they spoke) is the starting point. Remove '-ram', and add '-sse'. 'Falaram' gives 'fala' + 'sse', 'falasse'; 'comeram' gives 'comesse'; 'partiram' gives 'partisse'. The endings are '-sse' for 'eu', 'você', 'ele' and 'ela', '-ssemos' for 'nós', and '-ssem' for 'vocês', 'eles' and 'elas'; in the regions that use 'tu' the ending is '-sses'. 'Eu' and 'ele' have the same form, as in the imperfect indicative, so Brazilians keep the pronoun in these clauses ('Se eu fosse', 'Se ele fosse'). The spelling and stress of these endings, including the accent on the 'nós' form, are explained in the next note.

The 'eles' form of the preterite is the starting point because it shows the verb's stem, the part that stays when the person endings change ('fal-' in 'falo', 'falas', 'falaram'), so a verb with an irregular preterite stem ('tive-', 'fiz-', 'pud-', 'quis-') carries the irregularity straight through. The same memorized stem feeds three forms: the preterite, the future subjunctive and the imperfect subjunctive. Learn 'tiveram' and you also know 'tiver' and 'tivesse'. There is no verb that breaks this recipe: a verb that looks irregular here is simply irregular in its preterite. 'Pôr' gives 'puseram', 'pusesse'; 'trazer' gives 'trouxeram', 'trouxesse'; 'haver' gives 'houveram', 'houvesse'; 'ler' gives 'leram', 'lesse'.

Three pairs cause most errors. 'Ser' and 'ir' share 'foram' in the preterite, so they share 'fosse': 'Se eu fosse médico' ('ser') and 'Se eu fosse a Lisboa' ('ir'); context decides. 'Ver' and 'vir' are both irregular and differ by a letter: 'viram' gives 'visse' (see), 'vieram' gives 'viesse' (come). 'Dar' gives 'desse', which is also the contraction of 'de' + 'esse' (of that): 'Se ele desse' means 'if he gave', while 'o preço desse carro' means 'the price of that car'.

examples.target: Se eu falasse francês, trabalharia em Paris.
examples.source: If I spoke French, I would work in Paris.

examples.target: Se vocês comessem menos, dormiriam melhor.
examples.source: If you ate less, you would sleep better.

examples.target: Se nós tivéssemos um carro, iríamos à praia.
examples.source: If we had a car, we would go to the beach.

examples.target: Se ele fosse mais paciente, seria um bom professor.
examples.source: If he were more patient, he would be a good teacher.

examples.target: Se ela viesse, a festa seria perfeita.
examples.source: If she came, the party would be perfect.

examples.target: Se eles trouxessem o bolo, eu faria o café.
examples.source: If they brought the cake, I would make the coffee.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the -sse and -ssemos endings and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Spelling is a code for sounds, and a few facts explain every imperfect subjunctive ending at once. First, a single 's' between two vowels is pronounced like 'z' ('casa', 'coisa'). To write an 's' sound between vowels, Portuguese doubles the letter: 'ss', as in 'passo'. That is why 'fosse', 'falasse' and 'tivesse' are written with 'ss': the double letter keeps the sound sharp, like the 's' in English 'sip'. Second, a final unstressed 'e' is said like a short 'ee' (first lesson), so 'falasse' is fa-LAH-see. Third, 't' and 'd' before the sound 'i', which includes a final 'e' said 'ee', become 'ch' and 'j': 'tivesse' is chee-VEH-see, and the final '-de' of 'oportunidade' is '-jee'.

The stress follows the default rule from the lesson on stress. A word ending in 'e' is stressed on the second to last syllable, so 'falasse' is fa-LAS-se, 'comesse' is co-MES-se, 'partisse' is par-TIS-se. The stressed vowel is the one just before '-sse', and no accent is needed, because the word obeys the default of its ending. The 'vocês' and 'eles' ending '-ssem' ('falassem') is also stressed on the second to last syllable, which is what the ending 'em' predicts, so it needs no accent either.

The 'nós' form is different. The ending '-ssemos' adds a syllable after the stressed vowel, so the stress falls on the third to last syllable: fa-LAS-se-mos. The default for an ending in 'os' is the second to last syllable, so this stress breaks the default. A word stressed on the third to last syllable is a proparoxytone, and a proparoxytone always carries a written accent. The accent is therefore a stress mark, not decoration: without it a reader would apply the default and say fa-las-SE-mos.

The accent has a second job, because the choice between acute and circumflex records vowel quality (open or closed, first lesson). Regular verbs give 'á' for '-ar' verbs ('falássemos', open 'a'), 'ê' for '-er' verbs ('comêssemos', closed 'e') and 'í' for '-ir' verbs ('partíssemos'; 'i' has only one quality, so the acute only marks stress). Most irregular stems give an open 'é' ('tivéssemos', 'estivéssemos', 'fizéssemos', 'disséssemos', 'pudéssemos', 'quiséssemos', 'soubéssemos', 'viéssemos', 'déssemos'), 'ser' and 'ir' give a closed 'ô' ('fôssemos'), and 'ver' gives 'víssemos'. A stressed 'e' or 'o' with no mark can be open or closed, and spelling alone does not say which. This is why 'fosse', with no mark, is said with an open 'o' like the 'aw' of 'law' (FAW-see), while the circumflex of 'fôssemos' shows a closed 'o' like the 'o' of 'go' without the 'w' glide (FOH-se-mus). As with 'avó' and 'avô', the vowel quality belongs to the word, so learn the accent together with the form.

The same stress reason explains the conditional ending '-íamos' ('iríamos', 'moraríamos', 'ficaríamos'): the stress falls on the third to last syllable, so the 'i' carries the accent. The 'vocês' form '-iam' is different: 'iriam' is i-RI-am, stressed on the second to last syllable, which the ending 'am' predicts, so it has no accent. The other conditional forms ('viajaria', 'faria', 'seria') are stressed on the 'i' of '-ia', the second to last syllable, which the ending 'a' predicts, so they are written with no accent, like 'tia'.

The table applies the same method (divide, find the stress, read the default, compare) to the other new words of this unit, and adds the spelling facts they bring. The letter 'x' before a consonant sounds like 's' ('exterior', 'sexta'), but between vowels it has no rule, so you learn the word ('trouxessem' has the 'sh' sound). The letter 'g' before 'e' is the 'zh' sound, like the 's' in 'measure' ('coragem'), while 'g' before 'a' is a hard 'g' ('largar'). 'Qu' before 'e' is a 'k' sound with a silent 'u' ('quem'), while 'qu' and 'gu' before 'a' pronounce the 'u' as a 'w' glide ('quarenta', 'guardar', 'língua'). A 'ç' before 'a' is an 's' sound ('começar'), and so is 'c' before 'e' or 'i' ('conheceria', 'decisão'). The letter 'h' is silent ('hoje'), and 'lh', 'nh' and 'ch' are single sounds ('julho', 'sonho', 'chefe'). Finally, a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'a', 'e' or 'o' (with or without 's') takes an accent: 'tá', 'né', 'dê', 'prós', 'mês', 'já'.

grammar.title: Hypothetical conditions: se + imperfect subjunctive + conditional
grammar.explanation:
A conditional sentence has two parts: the clause introduced by 'se' (if), which states the condition, and the main clause, which states what follows. A clause is a group of words built around one verb with its own subject. Portuguese chooses the verb forms of both clauses according to how real the speaker considers the condition. English makes the same distinction with fewer forms, which is why it is easy to use the wrong one.

There are three degrees of reality. A habit or general truth takes the present indicative: 'Se chove, não saio' (If it rains, I don't go out). An open possibility about the future takes the future subjunctive in the 'se' clause, and the present, 'ir' + infinitive or the imperative in the main clause: 'Se eu tiver tempo, vou viajar'. English uses a plain present for this (If I have time, I'll travel), which hides the difference. An unreal or unlikely condition takes the imperfect subjunctive in the 'se' clause and the conditional in the main clause: 'Se eu tivesse tempo, viajaria'. Here English and Portuguese line up: 'had' corresponds to 'tivesse' and 'would travel' to 'viajaria'.

English marks the same split with its own tools: a present after 'if' for an open possibility (If I have time) and a past after 'if' plus 'would' in the main clause for an unreal one (If I had time, I would travel). Portuguese spends a different verb form on each degree.

The choice between 'tiver' and 'tivesse' depends on how likely the speaker thinks the event is, not on when it happens. Both can refer to tomorrow: 'Se eu tiver tempo' says it may well happen; 'Se eu tivesse tempo' says it is unlikely or imaginary. Unreal also covers the present: 'Se eu fosse rico' says that I am not rich. This tense does not describe an unreal past ('if I had won, I would have bought'); that needs a compound form taught in a later unit.

The main clause uses the conditional, in Portuguese 'futuro do pretérito', formed by adding '-ia', '-ia', '-íamos', '-iam' to the infinitive ('viajaria', 'comeria', 'partiria'), with 'faria', 'diria' and 'traria' irregular. It corresponds to English 'would' + verb. The imperfect subjunctive and the conditional are a matched pair: the first marks the condition as imagined, the second says what would follow. Never put the conditional after 'se'. 'Se eu teria tempo' is a typical error of English speakers, who carry over 'if I would'.

In everyday speech the main clause often uses the imperfect indicative ('Se eu tivesse tempo, viajava') or the imperfect of 'ir' plus an infinitive ('eu ia viajar', literally 'I was going to travel'). Both replace the conditional because they also view an event from a distance that is not the present. Only the main clause changes. In standard Portuguese the 'se' clause keeps the imperfect subjunctive. The two clauses can also swap places, in which case no comma is needed: 'Eu viajaria mais se tivesse tempo'.

'Se eu fosse você' is the standard way to give advice. You imagine yourself in the listener's place, which is an unreal situation because you are not that person, so the imperfect subjunctive is required. Literally it says 'if I were you'. It is softer than an order because it offers an opinion from the listener's own point of view. A variant is 'Se eu estivesse no seu lugar', literally 'if I were in the your place'.

grammar.title: Past requests and wishes: queria que, pediu que, esperava que
grammar.explanation:
A verb such as 'querer', 'pedir' or 'esperar' that introduces another event is called a trigger, and the clause after 'que' is the 'que' clause. It is a subordinate clause, meaning that it depends on the main clause. English usually uses an infinitive here (I want you to come, I asked her to wait). Portuguese usually puts a full verb with its own subject after 'que', in the subjunctive: 'Quero que você venha'. When the subject is the same, the infinitive stays, as in 'Queria viajar'.

The tense of the subjunctive verb is decided by the trigger. The two must line up in time. A trigger in the present ('Quero', 'Peço', 'Espero', 'É importante') takes the present subjunctive. A trigger in a past tense, the preterite or the imperfect ('Pedi', 'Queria', 'Esperava', 'Era importante'), or in the conditional ('Gostaria que', 'Seria bom que'), takes the imperfect subjunctive. This rule is called the sequence of tenses, in Portuguese 'correlação de tempos'. It is the past counterpart of the present subjunctive pattern: 'Peço que ele fique' becomes 'Pedi que ele ficasse'.

The imperfect subjunctive here does not say that the event is unreal. 'Ela pediu que eu esperasse na porta' is a real request, and I probably did wait. The tense only shows that the sentence is told from a past vantage point and that the 'que' clause is still something asked, hoped or doubted, not asserted as fact. In English the infinitive hides this, but in Portuguese the verb carries it.

The same tense gives a soft present-time request. 'Eu queria que você me ajudasse' means 'I would like you to help me', now. The past form adds distance, which here means politeness, just as 'Eu queria um café' is softer than 'Quero um café'. Compare the direct 'Quero que você me ajude' with the softer 'Eu queria que você me ajudasse'. The same pattern expresses a wish about something that is not happening: 'Eu queria que você me ligasse mais' means 'I wish you would call me more'.

Every trigger you already know for the present subjunctive works the same way in the past: 'pedir', 'querer', 'esperar', 'preferir', 'duvidar', and impersonal expressions such as 'era importante que'. In conversation, 'pedir' often takes 'pra' plus an infinitive instead ('Ela pediu pra eu esperar'; 'pra' is the spoken form of 'para'). The subjunctive version is more formal and more common in writing.

grammar.title: Wishes, possibility and comparisons: quem me dera, tomara que, talvez, como se
grammar.explanation:
A wish is an event the speaker does not assert as fact, so wishes take the subjunctive. The tense depends on how realistic the wish is. A wish that could come true takes the present subjunctive: 'Tomara que dê certo' (I hope it works out). A wish about something that is contrary to reality or remote takes the imperfect subjunctive. English draws the same line: 'I hope it works' versus 'I wish it worked'.

'Quem me dera' and 'quem dera' are fixed phrases that mean 'if only'. Word by word, 'Quem me dera' is 'who to-me had-given': 'quem' is 'who', 'me' is 'to me', and 'dera' is a leftover one-word form of 'dar' (give) that once meant 'had given'. In this phrase it has no separate meaning to learn. The underlying idea is 'who would grant me this?', said about something nobody will grant, which is why it expresses longing. An infinitive follows when the wisher is also the one who would do or have the thing: 'Quem me dera ter mais tempo'. If a different subject is named, or you want to name the subject, use a clause with the imperfect subjunctive: 'Quem dera eu pudesse viajar mais', 'Quem dera a gente pudesse voltar no tempo'.

'Tomara' is a similar frozen form built on 'tomar' (to take). Its original sense is no longer transparent, so learn 'tomara que' as a unit meaning 'I hope that'. Followed by the present subjunctive it hopes for something possible: 'Tomara que ele venha amanhã'. Followed by the imperfect subjunctive it suggests that the hope is remote or probably false: 'Tomara que fosse verdade' (I wish it were true). Alone, 'Tomara!' means 'Let's hope so!'

A 'se' clause can stand alone as an exclamation, with the result left unsaid: 'Ah, se eu pudesse voltar no tempo!' This is the conditional sentence of the previous note with its main clause dropped, and it needs the imperfect subjunctive for the same reason. Use the imperfect subjunctive whenever the wished situation is contrary to the present: 'Quem dera estivéssemos de férias' refers to a present fact, that we are not on vacation.

'Como se' means 'as if'. It compares the real situation with an imagined one, so it takes the imperfect subjunctive, even when the main verb is in the present or the past, as long as the imagined situation is simultaneous with the main verb: 'Ele fala como se fosse o dono' (He talks as if he were the owner). English keeps the same form in 'as if he were'. The subjunctive is what tells the listener that he is not the owner. An imagined situation that comes before the main verb needs a compound form, taught in a later unit.

'Talvez' (maybe) and 'quem sabe' (who knows, perhaps) present an event as a possibility, not a fact, so they usually take the subjunctive too, with the same tense logic as the rest of this note. The present subjunctive keeps the possibility open: 'Talvez ele venha amanhã'. The imperfect subjunctive is used when the possibility is imagined or depends on an unreal condition, or when the sentence is told from the past: 'Talvez eu me sentisse sozinha', 'Talvez desse certo se a gente tentasse'. 'Dar certo' means to work out, literally 'to give right'.

culture.title: Se eu fosse você, Mega-Sena and the Brazilian dream
culture.text:
The phrase 'Se eu fosse você', literally 'if I were you', is so familiar in Brazil that it became the title of a hit comedy film in 2006, in which a husband and wife swap bodies and see life from each other's point of view. The expression is the standard way to give friendly advice, and its softness is typical of Brazilian conversation: instead of saying 'You should accept', people say 'Se eu fosse você, aceitaria'.

Dreams about money are a national pastime. The Mega-Sena lottery, whose name refers to the six numbers drawn, draws huge crowds to lottery shops ('casas lotéricas') when the prize reaches a very high amount, and people ask each other 'Se você ganhasse, o que faria?' Two classic dreams are the 'casa própria' (owning your own home; literally own house) and the 'décimo terceiro salário' (literally the thirteenth salary), an extra month of pay that most formal employees receive in December and spend on gifts, debts or travel. 'Lotéricas', 'própria' and 'décimo' are all stressed on the third to last syllable, so each carries a written accent, as the lesson on stress explained.

Brazilians also use 'Quem me dera' and 'Tomara que' in songs and ordinary speech to talk about distant wishes. In conversation, the conditional is often replaced by the imperfect ('Se eu tivesse dinheiro, eu viajava'), a pattern that is natural in speech but less common in formal writing.

exercises.prompt: Match each imperfect subjunctive form with its verb
Why does 'falássemos' carry a written accent?
choices: It is stressed on the third to last syllable, which the ending 'os' does not predict
It shows that the 'ss' is pronounced like 'z'
It shows that the word is plural
exercises.explanation: The ending 'os' predicts stress on the second to last syllable. Stress on the third to last always needs a written accent.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of 'if we had'?
exercises.explanation: The stress is on the 'ves' syllable (ti-VÉS-se-mos), third to last, so the accent goes there. Irregular stems give an open 'e', hence the acute.

exercises.prompt: How is the 'ss' in 'fosse' and 'falasse' pronounced?
choices: Like 's' in 'sip'; the double 's' keeps the sound sharp
exercises.explanation: A single 's' between vowels sounds like 'z' ('casa'). Doubling it to 'ss' gives the 's' sound.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'fosse' need no written accent, although 'fôssemos' does?
choices: 'Fosse' is stressed on the second to last syllable, which the ending 'e' predicts; 'fôssemos' is stressed on the third to last, which no ending predicts
Accents are written only on forms ending in 'os'
exercises.explanation: A written accent appears when the stress breaks the default of the ending. 'Fosse' obeys it; 'fôssemos' does not.

exercises.prompt: How is 'x' pronounced in 'sexta' (short for 'sexta-feira')?
choices: Like 's' in 'sip', because 'x' before a consonant sounds like 's'
exercises.explanation: Before a consonant, 'x' is an 's' sound, as in 'exterior' and 'texto'. Between vowels there is no rule, which is why 'trouxessem' has the 'sh' sound and must be learned.

exercises.prompt: What does the 'u' of 'língua' sound like?
choices: A 'w' glide, because 'gu' before 'a' pronounces the 'u'
exercises.explanation: The 'u' is normally silent in 'que', 'qui', 'gue' and 'gui'. Before 'a' or 'o', as in 'língua', 'guardar' and 'quarenta', it is a 'w' glide.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'né' carry an accent although it has only one syllable?
choices: Because a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'e' takes an accent, which also marks the open 'e'
Because it ends in a nasal vowel
exercises.explanation: Stressed monosyllables ending in 'a', 'e' or 'o' take an accent ('né', 'tá', 'só', 'já'). 'Né' is short for 'não é'.

exercises.hint_source: I hope it's sunny tomorrow (it could easily happen). Verb: 'fazer'.
exercises.explanation: A realistic hope takes the present subjunctive: 'faça'. A remote hope would take the imperfect: 'fizesse'.

exercises.prompt_source: He talks as if he knew everything.

exercises.prompt_target: Ela fala como se ___ a dona da empresa.
exercises.hint_source: She talks as if she were the owner of the company. Verb: 'ser'.
exercises.explanation: 'Como se' compares reality with an imagined situation, so it takes the imperfect subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ele gasta como se fosse rico', the main verb 'gasta' is in the present. Why is 'fosse' not a present form?
choices: Because 'como se' compares reality with an imagined situation, whatever the tense of the main verb
Because the whole sentence is in the past
Because 'fosse' is the only form of 'ser' after 'se'
exercises.explanation: 'Como se' takes the imperfect subjunctive here, which marks the comparison as imagined. He spends like a rich man, but he is not one.

exercises.prompt_source: If only I had more free time!
If I were you, I wouldn't quit.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the kind of condition it expresses

pairs.target: Se eu tiver tempo, vou viajar.

exercises.audio_target: Se eu tivesse tempo, eu viajaria.
choices: If I have time, I will travel.
If I had time, I would travel.
When I had time, I traveled.

exercises.audio_target: Se nós comêssemos menos, dormiríamos melhor.
choices: If they ate less, they would sleep better.
If we ate less, we would sleep better.
If we eat less, we will sleep better.

exercises.audio_target: Eu queria que você viesse à festa.
choices: I want you to come to the party.
I hope you come to the party.
I wanted you to come to the party.

exercises.audio_target: Quem dera eu soubesse tocar piano.
choices: I know how to play the piano.
I hope I learn to play the piano.
I wish I knew how to play the piano.

exercises.audio_target: Se eu fosse mais corajoso, arriscaria mais.
exercises.hint_source: If I were braver, I would take more chances.

exercises.audio_target: Se nós tivéssemos tempo, iríamos à praia.
exercises.hint_source: If we had time, we would go to the beach.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, what would Tiago do if he won the lottery?
choices: Buy a house on the beach
Quit his job and travel the world
exercises.explanation: Eu largaria o emprego no mesmo dia e viajaria pelo mundo.

exercises.prompt: The words of 'valer a pena' literally say 'to be worth the pain'. What does it mean in natural English?
exercises.explanation: 'Pena' here is trouble or sorrow, so the phrase says that the result is worth the trouble.

exercises.prompt_source: If I had more time, I would travel more.
answers: Se eu tivesse mais tempo, viajaria mais.
Se eu tivesse mais tempo, eu viajaria mais.
Se eu tivesse mais tempo, viajava mais.
Se eu tivesse mais tempo, eu viajava mais.
Se eu tivesse mais tempo, ia viajar mais.
Se eu tivesse mais tempo, eu ia viajar mais.

exercises.prompt_source: If I were you, I would accept.
answers: Se eu fosse você, eu aceitaria.
Se eu fosse você, eu aceitava.
Se eu fosse você, ia aceitar.
Se eu fosse você, eu ia aceitar.

exercises.prompt_source: I wish I could travel more.
answers: Quem dera eu pudesse viajar mais.
Quem me dera eu pudesse viajar mais.
Quem me dera poder viajar mais.
Ah, se eu pudesse viajar mais!

exercises.explanation: A past trigger ('pedi') takes the imperfect subjunctive in the 'que' clause: 'esperaram' gives 'esperasse'. Spoken Portuguese often uses 'pra' plus an infinitive instead.
